turns.question: Where is the structural map engine implemented, and how is the parser engine selected per file?
turns.text:
The README already answers most of this. Let me confirm by reading `internal/mapengine/` directly.Now let me look at the actual engine selection logic and the map-building code.This confirms the engine-selection logic precisely. Now let's check the two mapper implementations and where `--map` is wired into the CLI/read path.Now let's check where CLI wires `--map`/`--map-engine` to this package, to confirm entry points.This confirms the entry point. I have everything needed.

## Answer

**Structural map engine location:** `internal/mapengine/` — four files implementing a `Mapper` interface with three concrete engines plus a router:

- `internal/mapengine/types.go` — shared types (`Engine`, `Options`, `Result`, `Symbol`), the `Mapper` interface, and the top-level `Map(path, content, opts)` dispatcher (types.go:125) plus the auto-routing logic `mapAuto` (types.go:143).
- `internal/mapengine/goast.go` — `GoASTMapper` (goast.go:11), uses Go's standard `go/ast` + `go/token` to walk top-level declarations (`goASTSymbols`, `goFuncDeclSymbol`, `goTypeSymbol`, `goGenDeclSymbols`).
- `internal/mapengine/treesitter.go` — `TreeSitterMapper` (treesitter.go:12), built on the `gotreesitter` library (imports `gotreesitter` + a `grammars` package), with per-language tag queries (`treeSitterEntry`, `languageConfigs`, `symbolFromTag`).
- `internal/mapengine/regex.go` — `RegexMapper` (regex.go:10), a line-pattern fallback with per-extension rule tables (`regexRules`, `rulesForPath`, `matchLine`).

**Parser engine selection per file** — done in `mapAuto` (`internal/mapengine/types.go:143-158`), keyed on the lowercased file extension:

```go
func mapAuto(path string, content []byte, opts Options) (Result, error) {
	switch strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(path)) {
	case ".go":
		result, err := GoASTMapper{}.Map(path, content, opts)
		if err == nil { return result, nil }
		fallback, _ := RegexMapper{}.Map(path, content, opts)
		fallback.Fallback = true
		return fallback, nil
	case ".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx", ".py", ".rs":
		return mapTreeSitterWithFallback(path, content, opts, false)
	default:
		return RegexMapper{}.Map(path, content, opts)
	}
}
```

- `.go` → `GoASTMapper`, with silent fallback to `RegexMapper` on error.
- `.ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.py/.rs` → `TreeSitterMapper` via `mapTreeSitterWithFallback` (types.go:160-171), which itself falls back to `RegexMapper` if tree-sitter errors (e.g. `ErrUnsupportedLanguage`) — warnings are only appended when `warnUnsupported` is true or the error isn't the "unsupported language" sentinel.
- Everything else → `RegexMapper` directly.

Selection can be overridden explicitly: `Map()` (types.go:125-141) honors `opts.Engine` when set to `EngineRegex` or `EngineTreeSitter` (bypassing the extension check), corresponding to the CLI's `--map-engine regex` flag. This matches the README's stated behavior verbatim.

**Wiring into the CLI:** `internal/ghx/read.go:186-192` — when `opts.Map` is set, it calls `mapengine.Map(path, []byte(text), mapengine.Options{Engine: ..., Level: ..., Kind: ...})`, passing through CLI flags `--map-engine`, `--map-level`, `--map-kind` (declared upstream in `internal/cli`, not individually inspected here).

**Not verified:**
- I did not open `internal/cli/ghx.go` or `code.go` to see the exact cobra flag definitions/plumbing for `--map`, `--map-engine`, `--map-level`, `--map-kind` — only confirmed via `read.go` that `opts.Map`/`opts.MapEngine`/etc. exist and feed into `mapengine.Map`.
- I did not read the full bodies of `goast.go`/`treesitter.go`/`regex.go` line-by-line (only structural maps), so internals like the tree-sitter tag-query definitions or the Go generics handling are taken from signatures/README claims, not fully inspected line-by-line.
- I did not check `internal/mapengine`'s test files (`regex_test.go`) or any tests in `internal/ghx` for behavioral confirmation beyond what's shown above.

README:
# ghx — GitHub Code Exploration for AI Agents

One command does what takes 3-5 API calls. Batch file reads, code maps, search — all via `gh` CLI. Write JS programs that compose operations in one round-trip.

## Why

An agent wants to understand `packages/shadcn/src/utils/` in [shadcn-ui/ui](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui):

**With `gh` CLI** — 4 turns, 4 API calls, reads 3 full files (3,761 tokens), sees 3 of 34 files:
```
gh api /repos/shadcn-ui/ui/contents/packages/shadcn/src/utils       → JSON with shas, urls, links (480 tokens for a file list)
gh api /repos/.../get-config.ts --jq '.content' | base64 -d         → full file (1,981 tokens — agent only needed exports)
gh api /repos/.../registries.ts --jq '.content' | base64 -d         → full file (676 tokens)
gh api /repos/.../frameworks.ts --jq '.content' | base64 -d         → full file (624 tokens)
```

**With ghx** — 2 turns, 2 API calls, maps 10 files (3,058 tokens), sees signatures of all 10:
```
ghx read shadcn-ui/ui packages/shadcn/src/utils                     → directory listing (199 tokens)
ghx read shadcn-ui/ui "packages/shadcn/src/utils/*.ts" --map        → signatures of 10 files (2,859 tokens)
```

Same token budget. The `gh` agent read 3 full files. The ghx agent saw the structure of 10 — imports, exports, function signatures — and knows which ones to drill into. Pass a file, get content. Pass a directory, get a listing. Pass a glob, get matching files. Same command, always useful output.
